title: Does an elephant burn like 160,000 mice?
hook: An elephant weighs as much as 160,000 mice. Does it burn as much energy as all of them?

knows: surface area grows more slowly than volume as things get bigger
animals burn food for energy even at rest
doesNotKnow: that resting energy use grows roughly as mass to the three-quarters power (Kleiber's rule)
that per gram, bigger animals burn far less

misconception: Energy use is proportional to body mass, so an animal 160,000 times heavier uses 160,000 times the energy.
objective: The learner can explain that resting energy use grows roughly as mass^0.75, so a 160,000-times-heavier animal uses about 8,000 times the energy in total and about 1/20 as much per gram.

claims.text: Across mammals, resting (basal) energy use grows roughly as body mass to the 3/4 power (Kleiber's rule).
claims.source: Kleiber M. (1932) Body size and metabolism, Hilgardia 6:315-353; West, Brown & Enquist (1997) Science 276:122-126.

claims.text: With a 3/4-power rule, an animal 160,000 times heavier uses 160,000^0.75 = 8,000 times the energy in total, and 160,000^-0.25 = 1/20 as much per gram.
claims.source: 160,000^0.25 = 20 exactly (20^4 = 160,000), so 160,000^0.75 = 20^3 = 8,000 and per gram 8,000/160,000 = 1/20. Recomputed in node (artifacts/scratch/w2life/check.mjs).

claims.text: Under the rule each tenfold step in mass multiplies total energy use by about 5.6 (10^0.75 = 5.62), not 10.
The exponent is debated: some analyses find nearer 2/3 for mammals' basal metabolism, and single species sit above or below the line.
claims.source: White C.R. & Seymour R.S. (2003) PNAS 100:4046-4049 (exponent about 0.686 for mammalian BMR); Dodds, Rothman & Weitz (2001) J. Theor. Biol. 209:9-27.

claims.text: The masses are rounded for the lesson: a 20 g mouse and a 3,200 kg elephant (160,000 times heavier). The animal is drawn not to scale; its glow is energy per gram relative to the mouse.
claims.source: Choice in Demo.tsx (RATIOS; size grows with log mass; fill opacity 0.1 + 0.9 x mass^-0.25). House mice weigh roughly 15-30 g; Asian elephants several tonnes, so 3,200 kg is a small elephant.

recall.question: Animal B weighs 10,000 times as much as animal A. Using the 3/4-power rule, roughly how much more energy does B use in total at rest?
recall.why: 10,000^0.75 = 1,000. Total use grows more slowly than mass, so per gram B burns a tenth as much as A.
